case.title: The Empty Seed Heads
case.hook: Same parent, two gardens. But there’s one more thing. When I opened the dry flower heads, Pot A’s were packed with seeds. Pot B’s, from the shady courtyard, were almost empty. I hardly ever see bees back there. So I set up a test, and I wrote everything on my data sheet.
case.question: Why were Pot B’s flower heads almost empty of seeds?
case.how: Find 4 clues as you work through the lesson. Then crack the case (solve it) at the top of the Assignment tab.

clues.t: A bee picks up pollen at one flower and rubs it off at the next. Only a flower of the same kind can use it.

clues.where: The Lesson, Part 1: the bag test
clues.t: Same sun, same water: flower heads with bees made lots of seeds; bagged heads made almost none. The bees were the difference.
Pollination comes first. No pollination means no fertilization, and no fertilization means no seeds.
Seeds travel away from the parent by wind, water, hitchhiking, animals eating them, or falling and being buried.

solve.title: What happened to Pot B?
solve.q: Which answer fits all four clues?

options.t: The seeds were there, but they blew away before Dr. Reyes looked.
options.why: Check Clue 2. In the bag test, the bagged heads never made full seeds at all, even with nothing blowing them away.

options.t: Almost no bees reached Pot B. Without bees carrying pollen between flowers, most tiny flowers were never pollinated, so they couldn’t be fertilized or make seeds.
options.why: Case cracked! The bag test proved it: same sun, same water, no bees, no seeds. Pollination comes first. Now write your case report: it’s the questions below.

options.t: Shady plants never make seeds, no matter what.
options.why: Check Clue 2: the bagged heads were in full SUN and still made almost no seeds. What did the bags keep out?

relay.afterText: The new plant inherits its traits
relay.title: Put the cycle in order
todo: Drag each step onto a station, or tap a step and then a station.
Start with what has to happen FIRST before a seed can exist.
Fill all five stations and watch a new plant come around.

why.t: The last step makes a new plant. When it flowers, the whole cycle starts again.

miss.0: Pollen has to move first. Nothing else can happen until it does.
miss.1: Pollen has to arrive before it can join the egg.
miss.2: A seed can only form after the egg is fertilized.
miss.3: A seed has to exist before it can travel.
miss.4: Sprouting is the last step, after the seed lands somewhere new.

relay.win: Around the cycle! Pollination → fertilization → seed → travel → germination. Then the new plant flowers, and it starts again. That’s a clue.

sort.afterText: Florida seeds travel in five ways
sort.subject: Florida seeds
sort.title: Seed travelers
todo: Drag it to the way it travels, or tap a card and then a way.

why.t: A seed that lands far from its parent has its own sun, water and space to grow.

cards.t: Red maple: each seed has a thin wing that spins like a helicopter.
cards.miss: A thin wing catches moving air. What carries it?

cards.t: Red mangrove: long, pencil-shaped seedlings drop into the water and float to new shores.
cards.miss: It floats. What carries something that floats?

cards.t: Spanish needles: tiny seeds with hooked prongs that stick to fur and socks.
cards.miss: Hooks grab onto things that walk by. Which way is that?

cards.t: Beautyberry: purple berries that birds eat. The seeds come out in their droppings far away.
cards.miss: Something swallows these. Which way travels inside an animal?

cards.t: Live oak: heavy acorns fall under the tree. Squirrels bury some and forget them.
cards.miss: These are too heavy to fly or float. They fall, and then an animal moves them.

sort.win: Five seeds, five ways to travel! Wings, floating, hooks, berries and buried acorns all get seeds away from the parent. That’s your last clue.

welcome.label: Welcome · the empty seed heads
welcome.script: It’s Dr. Reyes again. Remember my two pots? I opened the dry flower heads. Pot A’s were packed with seeds. Pot B’s, from the shady courtyard, were almost empty. And I almost never see bees back there. Is that a coincidence? I set up a test to find out. Look at my data sheet in the case file.

warmup.label: Warm-Up · pollen pass (Clue 1)
warmup.script: Time to be the bee. You start out dusty with sunflower pollen. Fly to another beach sunflower and watch the pollen rub off. One warning from the field: some flowers look a lot like beach sunflowers, but they aren’t. Look closely before you land.

vocab.label: Word Wall
vocab.notes: Say each word. For pollination, pretend to fly a bee from flower to flower.

part1.label: Part 1 · the bag test (Clue 2)
part1.script: Here’s my test. Same sunny garden, same water. On some flower heads, I tie a mesh bag. Air and sunlight get through, but bees can’t. Others stay open. You decide which heads get bags. Then wait three weeks and count the seeds. Bag at least one and leave one open, so it’s a fair test.

part2.label: Part 2 · put the cycle in order (Clue 3)
part2.script: Five steps make a new plant. Your job is to put them in order. Ask yourself: what has to happen before a seed can even exist? Start there. When all five are in place, watch a new plant come all the way around.

explore.label: Part 4 · seed travelers (Clue 4)
explore.script: Seeds can’t walk, but they sure do travel. Some fly. Some float. Some hitch a ride on your socks. Read each Florida seed card and figure out how it gets away from its parent. Look for clues like wings, hooks or berries.

assignment.label: Assignment · crack the case
assignment.script: Do you have all four clues? Crack the case at the top of this tab: why were Pot B’s flower heads empty? Then answer two questions, follow one flower through all five steps, and write your CER. Your answers save as you type.

evidence.label: Use your evidence · CER
evidence.script: A classmate says flowers are just for looking pretty. Hmm. Think about my bag test. What happened to the flower heads the bees couldn’t reach? Pick your side, tap two pieces of evidence in the planner, then explain how they prove your claim.

closing.label: Case closed
closing.notes: Celebrate; tease week 14 (life cycles and seasons).
closing.script: Case closed! My courtyard sunflower had plenty of flowers, but almost no bees, so almost no seeds. I’m planting more flowers back there to invite the bees in. Next week, we’ll follow Florida plants and animals through their whole lives, and through the seasons.

hlCoach.title: Highlight like a scientist
tips: Highlight key words, not whole paragraphs.
If everything is yellow, nothing stands out. Aim for a few words in each paragraph.
Look for words that are explained.
Bold words, and words followed by “means”, “is called” or a meaning in ( ), are often worth saving.
Look for answers to the Big Question.
Ask yourself: does this help me explain how animals notice and respond?
“Because”, “so” and “first … then” show how ideas connect.
Yellow = important. Green = evidence I might use in my answer. Pink = something I wonder about.

practice.q: Practice: tap the 3 to 5 words that matter most in this sentence.
practice.text: A bee carries pollen from one flower to another, so the flower can make seeds.
practice.model: A scientist might highlight “bee”, “carries pollen” and “seeds”. Those words carry the idea. Small words like “the” and “so” don’t.

hlCoach.outside: This works in every subject. When you read anything, save the words that answer your question, and skip the rest.
